title: The Four Quantum Numbers and the 2p Electron
notes: The four quantum numbers through one concrete example — the 2p electron of carbon — the fastest route to the 'write the quantum numbers' question. Definitions and the full metric table are in the main note and the metrics tab.

Carbon (Z = 6): 1s² 2s² 2p². Take a 2p electron: n = 2 (L shell, second energy level); l = 1 (p subshell, dumbbell shape); m = −1, 0 or +1 (which of px, py, pz the orbital is); mₛ = +½ or −½ (spin). Hund's rule puts the two 2p electrons in different p orbitals with parallel spins, so a valid full set for the first is n = 2, l = 1, m = −1, mₛ = +½ and for the second n = 2, l = 1, m = 0, mₛ = +½.
• **n:** shell, size and energy (r ∝ n²; capacity 2n²).
• **l:** subshell and shape (s spherical, p dumbbell, d clover, f complex); angular momentum √(l(l+1))·h/2π; permitted values 0 … n − 1.
• **m:** orientation in space; 2l + 1 values; explains Zeeman splitting.
• **mₛ:** spin ±½; Pauli exclusion follows — no two electrons share all four numbers.
### The validity ladder (check in this order)
n ≥ 1 → l ≤ n − 1 → |m| ≤ l → mₛ = ±½. So (n = 2, l = 2) is invalid (l = n), (n = 3, l = 2, m = −3) is invalid (|m| > l), and (n = 2, l = 1, m = 0, mₛ = ±½) is valid.

The three p orbitals are degenerate in a free atom; a magnetic field splits them (Zeeman). Filling follows Hund's rule: singly with parallel spins first — the origin of carbon's two unpaired 2p electrons and hence its divalent/paramagnetic behaviour.
confusion: ❌ mₛ determines the orbital orientation. ✅ mₗ gives orientation; mₛ gives spin.
❌ l can take the value n. ✅ l runs 0 to n − 1.
❌ Two 2p electrons of carbon must have opposite spins. ✅ Hund's rule: parallel spins in different degenerate orbitals first.

The letters s, p, d, f come from the old spectroscopic terms sharp, principal, diffuse, fundamental.
Pauli's exclusion principle is the reason any orbital holds at most two electrons.
examples: **Problem:** How many electrons in an atom can have n = 3 and m = 0? **Solution:** 3s (1 orbital, m = 0), 3p (one of three orbitals has m = 0), 3d (one of five) → 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 electrons.

summary: The four quantum numbers are best learned through one worked example, the 2p electron of carbon (Z = 6, configuration 1s² 2s² 2p²). For a 2p electron n = 2 (L shell, second level), l = 1 (p subshell, dumbbell shape), mₗ = −1, 0 or +1 (selecting px, py or pz) and mₛ = ±½ (spin). Hund's rule places the two 2p electrons in different p orbitals with parallel spins, so a valid full set for the first is (2, 1, −1, +½) and for the second (2, 1, 0, +½) — the two unpaired electrons that make atomic carbon paramagnetic. Validity is checked in a fixed ladder: n ≥ 1, then l ≤ n − 1, then |m| ≤ l, then mₛ = ±½, so (2,2,0,+½) and (3,2,−3,±½) are impossible while (2,1,0,+½) is allowed. The three p orbitals are degenerate in a free atom and split in a magnetic field.
importantConcepts: Worked example: carbon's two 2p electrons with sets (2,1,−1,+½) and (2,1,0,+½) by Hund's rule
n fixes shell and size (r ∝ n², capacity 2n²); l fixes subshell and shape (s, p, d, f) with 2(2l + 1) electrons
mₗ fixes orientation with 2l + 1 values; mₛ = ±½ fixes spin, so each orbital holds two electrons
Validity ladder: n ≥ 1 → l ≤ n − 1 → |m| ≤ l → mₛ = ±½
Degeneracy and Hund's rule: the three p orbitals fill singly with parallel spins, giving carbon two unpaired electrons
importantStatements: mₗ gives the orientation of the orbital while mₛ gives the spin; they are not interchangeable.
l runs from 0 to n − 1 only, so l = n is impossible.
Carbon's two unpaired 2p electrons make the atom paramagnetic and allow two covalent bonds after promotion.
A 3d electron has l = 2 and five m values (−2, −1, 0, +1, +2).
The letters s, p, d and f come from the old spectroscopic terms sharp, principal, diffuse and fundamental.

keyPoints: Answer in the order n → l → m → mₛ, checking validity as you go.
Orbital angular momentum is √(l(l+1))·h/2π, with l = 0 … n − 1.
Electrons with n = 3 and m = 0: 3s, 3p and 3d each allow one orbital with m = 0, so 6 electrons.
Pauli's exclusion principle is why no orbital holds more than two electrons.
specialNotes: Two electrons of carbon in 2p orbitals have parallel spins (Hund), not necessarily opposite ones.
px, py and pz are degenerate in the free atom; a magnetic or ligand field is needed to split them.
A complete state needs all four numbers — n and l alone do not identify an electron.
examShortTricks: Name the element and write its configuration first, then give one set per electron.
Invalid sets die at the first broken rung of the ladder — usually l = n or |m| > l.
For a d electron: l = 2, so m has five values and the subshell holds 10 electrons.
examNotes: 'Write the quantum numbers of the electrons of an atom' is a standard 3–4 mark question.
Testing sets for validity is the most common one-mark item in this topic.
Unpaired-electron counting from the configuration usually follows for the magnetism part.
